passage:
I sit next to Ritu in chemistry, so I've watched the whole thing. Sachin, in the next row, forgets everything: lab coat, homework, the day of the test. Some boys call him 'the Sieve'.
Ritu never joins in. She texts him the night before: 'Lab coat!' On Thursdays she sits with him in the library, just doing her own work while he does his, and he actually gets things done with her there. When he finished the chapter test early last week, she clapped quietly and said, 'Told you.'
Once I heard someone ask her, 'Does he have some problem?' Ritu said, 'I don't know, and it's not for us to decide. That's for doctors. He's trying. That's what I see.'

qa.q: What does Ritu text Sachin the night before?
qa.a: 'Lab coat!'

qa.q: How does Ritu feel about Sachin when someone asks if he has some problem?
qa.a: She feels protective and loyal towards him, refusing to guess at a label because that is for doctors, and saying, 'He's trying.'

qa.q: Which of Ritu's choices seems to help Sachin most, and why?
qa.a: Sitting with him in the library on Thursdays, each doing their own work, helps him get things done, along with gentle reminders and cheering small wins.

qa.q: How might Sachin feel when Ritu claps quietly and says 'Told you'?
qa.a: He may feel proud and believed in, especially compared with being called names by others.

grounding: Shows, through a classmate's eyes, a friend who never mocks forgetfulness, gives gentle reminders, studies alongside, celebrates small wins and leaves any diagnosis to professionals.

passage:
Week one: Kunal forgot his half of the group project slides, again. Swati was furious. 'Are you just lazy?' she snapped. His face went blank, and he didn't come to the next meeting.
Week two: Swati felt bad. This time she asked, 'What makes it hard?' Kunal shrugged. 'I start, then I lose track. I'm not trying to let you down.' So they tried something new: Swati set a shared reminder for the day before, and they worked side by side on a video call for an hour, each on their own slides.
Week four: Kunal finished his five slides a day early. Swati sent a thumbs-up and 'Proud of you.' He wrote back, 'First time ever. Same time next week?'

qa.q: How many slides did Kunal finish a day early?
qa.a: His five slides.

qa.q: What did Kunal's blank face after 'Are you just lazy?' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt hurt and ashamed, which is why he stayed away from the next meeting.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Swati helped Kunal?
qa.a: Asking 'What makes it hard?' instead of calling him lazy led to shared reminders and working side by side on a video call.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel reading 'Proud of you' from Swati?
qa.a: He may feel encouraged and valued, which is why he suggested the same time next week.

grounding: Shows a teenager moving from assuming laziness to respectful support: asking what is hard, gentle reminders, working side by side and celebrating a small win.

passage: Beta, you remind me of my friend Asif. At sixteen he forgot everything: his books, his homework, which day was the practical. The boys called him lazy. He wasn't; I saw him try harder than any of us. So I, Nilesh, started a small habit. Every evening I went to his house and we did homework at the same table, me doing mine, him doing his. I didn't help, just sat there. Somehow he could focus when I was beside him. I'd remind him, gently, "Physics file tomorrow." And when he finished a whole chapter, I'd clap like he'd scored a century. Years later a doctor explained a few things to him about how his brain worked. But first he just needed a friend at the table.

qa.q: What did Nilesh remind Asif about?
qa.a: "Physics file tomorrow."

qa.q: How did young Nilesh feel when the boys called Asif lazy?
qa.a: Nilesh felt it was unfair, having seen Asif try harder than anyone.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Nilesh began sitting beside Asif every evening, giving gentle reminders and celebrating each finished chapter.

qa.q: How might Asif have felt when Nilesh clapped?
qa.a: Asif probably felt proud and encouraged after being called lazy by others.

grounding: Shows a friend who refuses to call a forgetful classmate lazy, offering gentle reminders, company and praise, and leaving explanations to a doctor.

passage: With the board exams starting in six days and the hostel study room packed and noisy, Amandeep noticed that Neelam hadn't opened her chemistry book once. Neelam kept losing her notes, then her pen, then her place. Some girls muttered that she was lazy. Amandeep didn't believe it; she had seen Neelam stay up till two, trying. So she said, "Want to study together? You do your chapter, I'll do mine, same table." They sat side by side in the corner. Every forty minutes Amandeep said, "Water break," and they walked to the cooler. When Neelam finished her first full chapter, Amandeep high-fived her. "Told you." Neelam laughed, a little teary. Amandeep didn't guess at why it was hard for her. She just stayed.

qa.q: How many days were left before the board exams?
qa.a: Six days.

qa.q: What was Amandeep thinking when others called Neelam lazy?
qa.a: She felt protective and unconvinced, having seen Neelam stay up till two trying.

qa.q: What kind of support did Amandeep give?
qa.a: Studying side by side, regular water breaks and celebrating the first finished chapter, without guessing at a cause.

qa.q: How did Neelam feel after finishing the chapter?
qa.a: Neelam felt happy and moved, laughing a little teary.

grounding: Illustrates a friend who avoids assuming laziness and supports a struggling classmate with company, breaks and small wins.

passage: Chandrika had left her tuition-fees envelope on the bus again, and her mother was furious. "Lazy, careless, what will become of you?" Chandrika hid in her room. Her aunt Minakshi, staying with them that month, knocked with two cups of filter coffee. She didn't add to the scolding. "Want company while you do the maths set?" She sat at the other end of the desk with her own laptop work. Chandrika finished the set in forty minutes, a record. Minakshi smiled. "See? Nothing lazy about that." Later she gently suggested a sticky note by the door for important things. When Chandrika's mother wondered aloud if something was wrong with her, Minakshi said quietly, "Maybe talk to the school counsellor. Let the experts decide, not us."

qa.q: How long did Chandrika take to finish the maths set?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel after her mother called her lazy?
qa.a: She felt hurt and ashamed, hiding in her room.

qa.q: What did Minakshi do that showed respectful support?
qa.a: She sat beside her, praised the record time, suggested a sticky note and pointed the mother to the counsellor rather than guessing.

qa.q: How might Chandrika's mother feel after Minakshi's suggestion?
qa.a: She may feel calmer and more hopeful, with a proper next step instead of worry.

grounding: Shows an adult who doesn't assume laziness, offers company, reminders and praise, and leaves any diagnosis to professionals.

passage:
"You forgot your lab file again? So lazy," Arjun said, laughing, and walked off.
Salma stared at the floor. "Maybe he's right."
"He's not," said Seema. "You were up till midnight on that file. I saw your messages."
"Then why do I keep forgetting everything?"
"I don't know. I'm not a doctor. But if it bothers you, you could tell your mum and maybe see someone who actually knows."
"Maybe."
"Meanwhile, want to do homework on a video call tonight? I'll do mine, you do yours. We just keep each other company."
"That's it?"
"That's it. And I'll text you 'file' at seven every morning."
Two weeks later Salma held up her file at the gate. "Six days in a row!"
Seema clapped. "Six! Party!"
Salma grinned. "You're kind of amazing, you know."

qa.q: What did Seema promise to text Salma every morning?
qa.a: She promised to text "file" at seven every morning.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling when Arjun called Salma lazy?
qa.a: She felt protective and annoyed on Salma's behalf, sure Salma wasn't lazy because she had seen her messages from midnight.

qa.q: Which of Seema's choices helped, and why?
qa.a: She refused to assume laziness, offered company on a call and gentle reminders, and celebrated six days in a row, which built Salma up.

qa.q: How does Salma see Seema by the end?
qa.a: Salma admires Seema and feels grateful, calling her kind of amazing.

grounding: Seema doesn't mock Salma's forgetfulness, offers gentle reminders and company while working, celebrates small wins and leaves any diagnosis to professionals.
